Well, it's a CDProjektRed game. It has an interesting, visually distinctive, rich game world and the game is utterly contemptuous of the idea that anyone who is not a straight cis man might want to play in it. 

Let's start with the character creator. Your options are: burly man or petite sexy woman. There are more options for sexy woman than burly man. I came in wanting to make a butch woman, like my character in the TTRPG.  No. You cannot make butch, masc, curvy, fat, or even tall. You can adjust tit size. You can't make yourself or even your favorite singer.  You can make Harley Quinn. Oh. And you can give her a big or small penis. Hahahaha. She has a dong now.

So I gave up on that and decided to make a character who looks like someone from Skinny Puppy. You know, an actual goth punk. Nope. Can't do that, either. Face customization is...subtle, and the hair for men is universally tame. Oh yes. You can give him a vulva on his big burly body. 

There's really no roleplaying in the game either. There is one right answer to all dialog options and no responsiveness to different choices. Your V is just  not really customizable.

But,  I hear you arguing, you never really see your character in the game (you know, other than the times you see them naked or vulnerable), so why does it matter?  It matters in that I'm really not sure why they bothered. It's clear that the point of having female characters in this game is so the male player can leer at them, but you can't even play in 3rd person and stare at V's ass.  If there's no roleplaying and no flexibility on the character creator, why spend the resources on it at all?  Why not let people upload a bitmap portrait like in the old CRPGs? Why not lock the character as male like the Witcher. At least then there was an excuse for the ubiquitous misogyny in the game world because you were seeing it through Geralt's eyes and desires. I'm used to playing straight guys. I play video games. I'm not used to hearing hype about how inclusive a game is and finding out that it's inclusion as conceived by a fifteen year old boy, who thinks it's a joke.

And the game world is sexist. two thirds of the billboards in the game are some sort of sexy woman with her legs spread sucking on something. I'm stuck in a room with a holographic pole dancer with no head just tits and ass for one of the longer exposes at the beginning of the game. Half the characters talk to you like you're in a porno for no reason at all. Yes, I know this is a world inspired by Bladerunner and Total Recall and 80s punk aesthetic. The TTRPG world isn't like this, and even Bladerunner limited itself to one or two sexy billboards. Bladerunner's cyborg sex workers had curves and actual punk hair.

The game is fun enough, and the story is interesting, and I spent sixty bucks on it, so I'll sink some hours in it, but I won't be in love with it and I probably won't buy their next effort.

If you want to enjoy this fantasy as a woman, or a trans person, or really any of the stereotypically portrayed ethnic groups in the game, you should look ANYWHERE else.  Or,   just accept the fact that this is a game that is for straight guys and the game is aggressive about sending that message.

The game itself is alright. Just alright. For an AAA title from people that made Witcher series this doesn't quite cut it, now does it? The original release of this game was a total mess, so I waited and waited till everything was done and patched to even try it. I like cyberpunky aesthetic and feel, if nothing else, experiencing that vibe in this game would be alright.

I must say, the strong suits of this title are the. . . Segments with Johnny. Stealth approach trying to not alert the enemies and using your 'magic' (quickhacks) to manipulate stuff in game.

The weak suits are the combat itself (it's too easy and not challenging at all), stories that don't involve johnny or his insights (he's a colorful character that while crude, has a proper main character energy), driving (it feels off), bugs that are still in the game - there are a lot.

While bugs themselves don't outright softlock you and aren't game breaking, there's a ton of them. From bad rendering, to enemies phasing through stairs and catwalks, to vehicles spawning and despawning while you look, vehicles with enemies falling out of the sky and exploding on impact with the ground because you walked out a bit too far from their rendering , the vehicle you own spawning in unreachable places or places it can't leave from. . . There's a ton. I played a 'vanilla' experience naively thinking I wouldn't see all that mess. I was wrong. Perhaps there are mods improving those aspects, there should be some at this point anyway. 

The game itself is rather boring. The moment you realize your build you locked yourself into doesn't utilize quickhacks but has to rely on some other cyberware (part of equipment you 'wear') it becomes extremely straightforward and frankly, way too easy. I couldn't for the love of me sit through all the extra side content. I would physically die of boredom, so to leave an honest review, I rushed to the ending.

It's a blessing I could stick with the game for 117hrs but that's just because of my willpower to see it through and perhaps find something that's suddenly making this 6/10 game into 8 or 9. Sadly, in my case there was nothing of the sort.

Play if you must or otherwise feel compelled to, but only after getting it on sale. Don't have regrets for wasting money on something that was hyped out of the orbit and underdelivers.

**Not Recommended: I waited six years for this game to work.**

I was a day-one buyer of Cyberpunk 2077. I was there for the launch, and I swear I encountered just about every bug that ended up documented online.

So I waited.

I saw what CD Projekt Red had done with The Witcher 3 over time, and I genuinely believed Cyberpunk would get the same treatment. I wanted to experience this game when it was finally ready, rather than ruin my first playthrough fighting through technical problems.

Six years later, I still can't play it.

For me, it's the infamous audio crackling/popping glitch. If you've searched for this problem, you already know the worst part: everyone seems to have a different "fix," which means there really isn't one.

I've changed audio refresh/sample rates. Updated and reinstalled drivers. Turned SFX down and completely off. Disabled spatial audio. Used Windows spatial audio. Tried Bluetooth headphones, wired headphones, laptop speakers, desktop speakers, and monitor speakers. I've verified the game files, uninstalled and reinstalled the entire game, restarted the computer, turned it off and back on, and done all the other obligatory troubleshooting steps. I've gone through forums, Reddit threads, videos, and troubleshooting guides.

Believe me, if you're about to suggest a fix, I've probably tried it.

And before someone points at my Steam playtime as proof that the game must have been playable, those hours are extremely misleading. A huge amount of that time was spent with the game running while I was trying to troubleshoot the problem, testing settings, restarting, loading back in, driving around to see if the crackling returned, and repeating the process. Yes, there were stretches where I actually got to play the game, but I'd estimate maybe 25% of my recorded hours were spent genuinely playing rather than trying to make the game work.

And that's what makes this so disappointing. I *want* to play Cyberpunk 2077. I bought it at launch, watched CDPR spend years rebuilding its reputation, watched the game receive major updates and an expansion, and deliberately waited to give it the experience I thought it deserved.

But I've never once been able to actually play through the game.

Six years of patches, updates, fixes, and second chances, and a game-breaking audio issue that has been reported by players for years still makes the game effectively unplayable for me.

So, for the final time, I'm uninstalling Cyberpunk 2077. At this point, I have to accept that I'm probably never going to finish what I genuinely wanted to be a superb game.

I'm sure Cyberpunk 2077 is a great game when it works. I genuinely wish I could have found out.

6 years later and on patch 2.31, a lot of people like to say they've "fixed" the game now.
Well, you can patch the bugs, you can rework your god-awful skill tree, inventory and crafting mechanics.
You can add police that actually chase you, quests that actually function and cars that actually handle like cars.
They did all that in an attempt to "make things right", which I'll acknowledge.
But one thing you can't patch is the terrible, TERRIBLE writing.
They don't even give you the ability to skip dialogue until you've gone through the motions of a completely rail-roaded THREE HOUR LONG prologue every time you want to replay the game (or pick a premade character to start at Phantom Liberty, but doing so hamstrings you if you aren't playing a hacker). 
WHY can't you skip dialogue in the prologue? ♥♥♥♥ you, I guess.
The main plotline with the engram is just plain bad. It saps so much player choice out of V's character, and of course there's tolerating Johnny Silverhand.
My God, Johnny Silverhand. With Michael Pondsmith's tabletop character they actually managed to make Keanu Reaves not just unlikable, but insufferable.
You might even find yourself asking just how much of the time CDPR spent consulting with Pondsmith was concerning the game world and how much was spent on faithfully recreating his annoying rockerboy avatar in the video game, complete with a soundtrack that makes you question how this rockerboy ever had a fan base in the first place. Seriously, if SAMURAI were a real band that had to stand on their own merit independent of the game they'd struggle to break 100 views on youtube. "Chippin' In" is one of the worst songs I've ever heard in my life.
And if you thought Silverhand was bad enough they somehow lower the bar further in Phantom Liberty with Songbird, the Mary-Sue the DLC revolves around, who the game treats as a tragic heroine who can do no wrong despite her being another generally awful self-insert and the architect of all her own problems.
Gameplay wise the game is fine.
Combat is engaging with a decent amount of depth once you've gotten yourself a loadout of weapons and cyberware you like, but if you're playing a hacker the gameplay loop is extremely boring and tedious (scan a guy -> dump hacks -> he dies -> scan next guy -> repeat until entire room is dead and you didn't even need to draw any of those guns you went to the trouble of getting).
The voice acting is broadly competent. There are some stand out characters that are well voiced, but again the material they're working with is not ideal. Male V's voice is fine. Competent, unremarkable but not annoying either. Female V's  voice however is just bad. The voice actress they chose for her has two modes: "Make my voice quiver a bit and ham it up" for any scene that is even vaguely dramatic and "sassy girl boss" for anything else. This can get quite annoying given that this is the character your stuck with for the entire game.
Itemization is still all over the place, with certain paths giving objectively superior rewards which further limits replayability (for example siding with Songbird in the DLC gets you the single most overpowered piece of cyberware in the game, while siding with Solomon gets you an ok pistol and a mediocre cyberdeck).
As for role playing, this is not a role playing game.
V is a fixed character, you can choose whether they're male or female and you can make some morality choices here and there but generally your decisions don't have a huge amount of impact on the game.
The stock endings are all quite unsatisfying, Phantom Liberty adds some new ones in what seems to be an attempt to address this, but they're not much better.
I'd give it a 6.5/10 in it's current state, which is unlikely to change as CDPR seem to consider the myriad problems the game still has to be resolved now and they've long since moved on to botching their next game. I shan't be trusting CDPR again, the people who were responsible for the quality of their previous titles are either long gone or simple don't care anymore.

DISCLAIMER:
The game is definitely worth buying if you can get it at a massive discount, as in: single-digit price, being that one cannot deny that it is not a complete miss after the massive overhaul and fixes which polished what they could from the infamous initial version.

PROS:
The game obviously had a AAA budget and a fairly long story.
Someone poured their love for the Cyberpunk lore into the concepts and the pre-release marketing promised to deliver it.
If you want to end up with a mindless time-skip in the form of a semi-idle walk-and-click in your Library, this is a good choice. But again: only and only at a massive discount.

CONS:
1. Before anything else, the first thing that destroys the fun in this are the *unskippable* segments.
[spoiler] After Chapter 1 , you are thrown into an unskippable walking simulator with horrendous overeasy gameplay, that suffocates you with hopes of ending every time there is a fade-to-black, but no! At several points you have to literaly press the forward button several times to (!)crawl forward [/spoiler].
And the dialogue skip option is intentionally taken away at instances where you just sit and look at a character the developers deemed to be so important that you cannot skip.
Do you have choices? None that affect the gameplay.

And this can eat up to 15+ minutes of your life at several instances.

2. The gameplay is a an enormous tease and a letdown. You grow powerful incredibly fast and are given such a vast array of ways to combat that I had stopped upgrading my character a tad bit into chapter 2 because I couldn't find a reason to. The enemy AI is atrociously bad and unchallenging, the weapon classes are a gimmick (one even removes the need to aim at all, scoring instant headshots at a click of a mouse) and at first I thought the driving physics were some sort of an in-game joke.

3. The "cyberpunk" starts and ends with cosmetics in an illogical world that is simply any GTA-like space of copy-paste design, but you get to have a universal remote in your eyes.
The characters are unbelievable and the dialogues are cringe-inducing, with propaganda and forced perspectives infused with varying subtlety.

4. The game-breaking bugs that made it infamous are largely removed, but still present. At certain points the loading screen will shut down the game, there are untested spaces where you can get trapped and have to reload, the physics quirks are still present although rare, etc.

I really wanted to like the game and read online review promising the gameplay to get better as time progresses, but even this much time invested in it later, I cannot say that it is a win.
Unless, I repeat, you are to get it at a *large* discount.

I don't hate Grand Theft Auto V. I had fun with it, but after 239.4 hours, I eventually realized how repetitive the experience had become. GTA V was once something I could easily spend hours playing, but over time, the appeal faded & the game started feeling less like entertainment and more like an endless checklist.

GTA Online has an enormous amount of content, but that doesn't necessarily make all of it meaningful. You earn money, buy something, use it to earn more money, unlock another item, complete another activity, then repeat the same process. There is always another vehicle, property, business, outfit, weapon, cosmetic, event, achievement, or collectible waiting for you.

Eventually, I started asking myself: what am I actually working toward?

The biggest problem is the pursuit of exclusive & rare content. GTA Online has accumulated years of limited-time items, event rewards, promotional content, rare vehicles, clothing, liveries, tattoos, collectibles & other items. Some can still be obtained through specific requirements or returning events, while others have been removed or are no longer normally obtainable.

That creates a strange situation where someone can spend hundreds of hours trying to build the "perfect" collection, only to discover that something they wanted was tied to an event from years ago.

If the item is no longer obtainable, there is no amount of grinding that can get it back.

That's what makes the completionist mentality particularly frustrating. You're not simply trying to finish a game. You're trying to keep up with an ecosystem that has been evolving for years, while some of its history is permanently locked behind time-limited availability.

And even the items that remain obtainable can require an enormous investment of time.

For example, GTA Online's money-making activities often involve cooldowns, preparation missions, travel, matchmaking, setup, completion, & repetition. Even one of the game's major solo money-making activities has a cooldown between finales. Multiply that type of waiting & repetition across the countless things a player might want to purchase, unlock, or collect, and the hours add up very quickly.

My 239.4 hours alone equal roughly 9.98 full days of continuous time.

That's almost ten entire 24-hour days of my life spent inside Los Santos.

And that's only the recorded gameplay time.

It doesn't include time spent researching how to obtain items, watching guides, waiting for events, comparing prices, sitting through loading screens, or deciding what to do next.

That's where the opportunity cost becomes impossible for me to ignore.

I'm not saying video games need to be productive. They're entertainment, and entertainment has value. But once a game stops being entertaining & you're continuing only because you've already invested so much time, it becomes worth asking whether that time is better spent elsewhere.

GTA Online can make that especially difficult because there is always something else to obtain.

You can never quite be finished.

Another update arrives.

Another vehicle is released.

Another business becomes available.

Another event begins.

Another exclusive item appears.

Another achievement becomes something to chase.

Then the cycle starts again.

One sequence of the game eventually replaces another.

And eventually, Grand Theft Auto VI will replace this generation's attention with a new world, new characters, new gameplay systems, new content & potentially another online ecosystem to explore. Rockstar currently lists GTA VI for November 19, 2026.

That's not a criticism of GTA VI. It's simply the natural progression of the franchise.

My concern is how much time people can spend trying to completely exhaust an older game before moving on.

You could spend hundreds of hours collecting vehicles, grinding money, unlocking cosmetics & pursuing exclusives, only for the next Grand Theft Auto to arrive & give everyone another massive world full of things to collect.

The sequence never really ends.

That's why I'm no longer interested in chasing every GTA V exclusive simply because I don't have it.

If an item is available, great.

If I miss it, I'm not going to let a virtual item dictate how I spend my time.

Some people genuinely enjoy collecting everything, and that's perfectly fine. But for me, the collection itself eventually became more burdensome than rewarding.

I also don't think GTA V deserves to be treated as a bad game because of this criticism. It has had an enormous impact on gaming, GTA V's single-player campaign remains memorable, & GTA Online has maintained an extraordinary amount of content for years.

My criticism is much simpler:

There is such a thing as having too much of a good thing.

After 239.4 hours, the repetition became difficult to overlook.

The game went from:

"What should I do today?"

to:

"What else do I still need to unlock?"

That distinction matters.

At some point, you're no longer playing because you genuinely want to. You're playing because there's another box left unchecked.

And I don't want a game to become a second job.

My last session was December 2, 2024, and I'm comfortable leaving it there.

I don't regret every hour I spent in GTA V. I had fun, experienced the world, played with other people & made memories. But I also recognize that my time has value, and I don't want to spend hundreds more hours chasing increasingly obscure items simply because the game provides an endless list of things to obtain.

Grand Theft Auto V was fun, but it became repetitive.

GTA Online has more content than most players could reasonably exhaust, yet that abundance can also become the problem.

With GTA VI arriving, I'm choosing not to spend more of my time trying to complete an ecosystem that was never designed to truly end.

I do not recommend it anymore.

[h3]The Ultimate Nostalgia Trip, But Make It 60 FPS[/h3]
If you had told me back in 2013, huddled over a humming, overheating PlayStation 3 with the original dualshock clacking away, that I would one day be cruising down the Vinewood Hills at a buttery-smooth 60 frames per second on Steam, I probably would have cried.

Back on the PS3, GTA V was a technical marvel. We all stared in awe at the sun setting over Los Santos, forgiving the occasional texture pop-in, the 30 FPS drops during massive explosions, and the agonizingly long loading screens where you could easily go make a sandwich while Trevor was loading in. It was a masterpiece of its generation.

Fast forward to playing it on Steam, and it feels like meeting an old friend who just got a massive glow-up.

[h3]What’s Better on Steam?[/h3]
[list]
[] [b]Performance & Fidelity:[/b] Going from the console versions of the past to a modern PC setup is night and day. The draw distances, the crisp 1080p/4K resolution, and the fluid frame rates breathe entirely new life into a world I thought I knew by heart.
[] [b]Mods & Customization:[/b] While the vanilla game is fantastic, the PC modding community is the real MVP. Whether it's graphical overhauls, quality-of-life tweaks, or just messing around, it adds endless replay value.
[*] [b]Seamless Convenience:[/b] Having it right in your Steam library alongside your achievements, screenshots, and friends list makes jumping back into Los Santos effortless.
[/list]

[h3]The Verdict[/h3]
Coming back to this game after years away feels weirdly comforting. Sure, the radio ads are permanently burned into my brain, and I can still navigate the map blindfolded, but the charm hasn't faded one bit. Michael, Franklin, and Trevor are just as chaotic and entertaining as they were a decade ago.

If you’re on the fence about double-dipping or jumping over from the old console days, do it. It’s a nostalgic masterpiece that still holds its own, and experiencing it without the hardware limitations of 2013 is the ultimate way to play.

I've played only a little over 8 hours by the point I began writing this review. Here are my thoughts:

Pros:
This game looks amazing, it has a great voice acting, sfx and music. Character customization is unbelievably vast and really thought through. The setting is interesting, some of the mechanics I've come across so far are also good (like different origin stories for your character, etc.). There seems to be a lot of things you can do, but I can't really judge that, since I've only played it a little and couldn't properly explore the entire game. Story overall also looks promising, although I can't really judge that either with 8 hours of gameplay.

Cons:
Now to the cons, which for me are currently overweighting the cons. The game feels clunky. The driving is awful, it is probably the worst driving I've seen so far, feeling even worse than FC3, which already was a pain in the ass for me. The gunplay is massively underwhelming in my opinion. Like how the hell am I dumping 3 shotgun mags into someone's head and they are still alive? Enemies are extreme bullet sponges and that just ruins the experience for me. Also, the guns feel really unresponsive and the melee is just sliding around the room, slashing at people without much depth. The dialogues are really long and "draggy". The quests so far have not really felt rewarding and were rather boring. Some of the mechanics, like braindancing, were just straight up immersion-breaking for me. It took so long to finish the first braindance quest that I straight up don't want to ever experience it again. It was an interesting idea, I don't deny that, but overall it just feels dull. 

With that being said, I currently can't recommend the game. I wish I could give it a neutral score, especially since I can see the good things it has to offer. I really wanted to give it a shot and like the game, but I currently don't have enough time on my hands to force myself into playing a game that doesn't really entertain me, hoping it gets better soon. It is my personal preference though and I can deffinitely see why some people love this game so much. For me, it just didn't feel worth to continue.

I am a huge CDPR fan, especially because of The Witcher games, in which I've invested hunderds of hours across different platforms, but these games just felt rewarding, the story was gripping, the setting was even better (for me personally) and I didn't mind spending so much time on it. With Cyberpunk2077 I can't really say the same. Chances are that I will eventually change my review later, if I ever get to a point of giving it another shot, in the future, but currently I will just leave it be.

Game is good if you make it quick. Because the more you play, the more flaws and inconsistencies you'll notice.

- Still filled with bugs, most of it are physics and visual related( random flares after exiting map view, falling through the map, bosses/enemies stuck in invisible terrain, animation loop, civilian cars randomly blow up when nothing is happening, etc...) while none are game-breaking, it's simply incompetence for a game to have this many bugs considering it been out for more than half a decade, people says it's a lot better now compared to at launch, but it was a hot mess of garbage back then, which is a very low bar to pass. If you are someone who likes to mod your games and stuff, expect even more bugs.

- Throughout the game you will encounter a plethora of dialogue choices, some will affect the outcome of the mission, your relationship with certain NPCs, and even the ending of the game. Sadly, these instances are only the minority and 95% of the time these choices are meaningless, A/B/C/D simply bring you to the same outcome, they even hit you with these when there's only one option available. Instead of just let the conversation flow smoothly and represent you the options when it really matters, they constantly hit you with the illusion of choice and leave you wonder whether your decision have any weight to it or simply just a mean to an end.

- A massive amount of side quests, similar to dialogue choices, some of these will affect NPCs relationship and endings while the rest are straight up boring, have zero substances and just a reason for you to explore the map, level up and get some gears, and the open world aspect amplify this further, ignore the pointless quests, and suddenly the map looks empty, at least the views are good.

- Gameplay overall is fine except for close up combat which feel unpolished and unresponsive, like a random game in its alpha state and again, the game been out for years, there's no excuses for this. Looting is also buggy, some items can only be picked up at a certain angles, same thing with interacting with objects and scanning.

- Etc... and the DLC also have all of this problems.

Still worth it if on sale I suppose. And if you want to level up or get certain equipment, just get it from CET and stick to the main and related side quests. Again, the more you play, the worse it gets.

Cyberpunk 2077 might be the first game I've played where I genuinely enjoy the characters, world, story and combat while simultaneously wanting to launch the entire installation into the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ sun.

The vanilla character customization is embarrassingly shallow for a game whose entire setting revolves around modifying the human body. Night City is full of people with cybernetic limbs, mechanical jaws, artificial skin, exposed hardware and insane body modifications. Meanwhile V gets some lines on his face and apparently we're supposed to go, “Yep, I'm a cyborg now.”

So naturally, I went to mods.

That was a mistake.

Want cybernetic arms? Great. Download the arms.

Except you also need a framework.

And another framework.

And a cyberware core.

And an equipment system.

And an Atelier system.

Then you launch the game and discover the store exists BUT THE ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ ARMS AREN'T IN IT because apparently you downloaded the framework for the arms, the store for the arms, the system for equipping the arms, and everything else required to contemplate the philosophical concept of an arm — except the actual ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ arm.

Quit game. Nexus. Download. Vortex. Deploy. Launch game.

Now there are six stores.

Four are empty.

WHY ARE THEY THERE?

Install more mods to populate them.

Quit game. Nexus. Download. Vortex. Deploy. Launch game.

Want gauges? Same ♥♥♥♥.

Want facial cyberware? Same ♥♥♥♥.

Want clothes that don't look like V dressed himself by blindly sprinting through a futuristic Goodwill? Welcome back to Nexus.

And God help you if you install a giant mod collection hoping somebody else has already assembled all this into a coherent package. I tried that. I ended up with 300+ mods, stores containing nothing, stores containing nothing but shoes, mountains of Fem V cosmetics I couldn't use, dependencies for mods I didn't want, and absolutely no ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ idea which piece of this Jenga tower was responsible for what.

I eventually deleted the collection and discovered I'd spent more time modding Cyberpunk than playing Cyberpunk.

The frustrating part is that underneath all this ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, I actually like the game. I care about these characters. Panam is fantastic. Night City is incredible. When the combat and cyberware fantasy clicks, it's awesome.

That's precisely why this pisses me off so much.

A game called CYBERPUNK should not require an undergraduate degree in ArchiveXL, TweakXL, RED4ext, redscript, Codeware, Equipment-EX, CET, Virtual Atelier and whatever other technological incantation I've forgotten just so my character can LOOK LIKE A ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ CYBORG.

The modding community has produced some genuinely incredible work, and individual mod authors clearly put enormous effort into it. But the user experience of the Cyberpunk modding ecosystem is atrocious. Dependencies stacked on dependencies, content separated across downloads, storefronts separated from merchandise, inconsistent installation methods, and documentation that frequently assumes you already understand the ecosystem.

After hours of troubleshooting, installing, uninstalling, launching, quitting, relaunching and wondering why another ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ store is empty, I have reached enlightenment:

Maybe the real cyberpsychosis was the mods we installed along the way.

10/10 Panam.

9/10 Night City.

2/10 character customization.

0/10 second job as an unpaid Night City systems administrator.

The Death of The Cayo Perico Heist: How Rockstar Methodically Killed the Only Fair Content in GTA Online
When The Cayo Perico Heist dropped in December 2020, GTA Online players felt like they could finally breathe. After years of forced cooperative misery, mental breakdowns caused by unreliable random players, and outrageously overpriced properties, Rockstar finally delivered something that felt too good to be true: a highly lucrative heist that could be played entirely solo.

Cayo Perico was the ultimate symbol of freedom in Los Santos. You didn’t have to beg anyone to join, and you didn’t have to waste hours on tedious setups. You could jump in, pull off a slick stealth run, and pocket $1.3 to $1.8 million in just over an hour.

But then, Rockstar realized that players were actually having fun, and—more importantly in their eyes—they weren’t buying Shark Cards anymore. That’s when the methodical, ruthless, and shameless nerfing of the heist began, turning El Rubio's island into a frustrating, low-paying chore.

The Rap Sheet: How a Jackpot Was Turned into Spare Change
1. The Desecration of the Pink Diamond and Primary Targets
We used to cheer when we saw the pink diamond on the security cameras, knowing we were in for a massive payday. Today, Rockstar has practically stripped these targets of their value. Slashing the value of the Pink Diamond—sometimes dragging the total payout of a solo run down toward the $900k mark—is a massive slap in the face to the player's time. Why risk your neck against a private army when you walk away with barely more than what a basic VIP contract used to pay?

2. The Systematic Punishment of Solo Players (The Cooldown Terror)
The most hostile move was the execution of the solo playstyle. If you complete the heist alone, the game now forces a brutal 3-game-day cooldown (approx. 2 hours and 24 minutes) before you can start it again. Meanwhile, team play has a much shorter cooldown. This isn’t "game balance"; it's blatant extortion: “Play with others (who will take a cut of your money), or wait hours to play again.”

3. Guards Suddenly Became Mind-Reading Geniuses (Wallhack AI)
Stealth was the beating heart of Cayo Perico. You followed your memorized route, quietly took out the guards, and slipped away unnoticed. But Rockstar rolled out an update where guards now detect dead bodies. While this sounds good on paper, GTA Online’s notoriously buggy, decade-old AI turned it into a disaster. Guards now frequently see through solid walls or spot corpses on the completely opposite side of the map. Precise stealth has been replaced by a frustrating, unpredictable gamble.

4. Jacked-Up Setup Fees
Just to make absolutely sure you don’t keep too much of your hard-earned cash, they quadrupled the heist setup fee from $25,000 to $100,000. Before you even set foot on the island to scout, you start in the negatives, all while your final payout is actively being gutted.

Verdict: A Monument to Corporate Greed
The current state of the Cayo Perico Heist is a perfect mirror of what GTA Online has become: a game that is no longer designed to entertain you, but to frustrate you into opening your real-world wallet.

They took away the freedom, they took away the fair pay, and they replaced it with a buggy, soul-crushing grind. Rockstar didn't just ruin El Rubio's island; they sabotaged their relationship with their own community. This isn't game development—it's highway robbery.

I typically don't write negative reviews but I was so disappointed in this expansion I had to share my thoughts. The writing, narrative and gameplay of this expansion are garbage. The game looks great, some voice acting is pretty good, but the overall story telling and what the game actually has you doing in-between dialogues is not good or fun.
  There is an immediate shift in mission design and tone upon reaching the DLC zone. The whole narrative pov doesn't make sense. Are the npcs talking to "we the player", who knows about future events in the story or is it "V the street kid with Keneau Reeves in his head"? The characters seems to constantly be breaking the forth wall and speaking to the player with knowledge that the character V wouldn't have any way of knowing and this makes it very difficult to get invested at all in what is happening and I felt like a passive observer of a bad tv show, not an active participant in an immersive story and world.
  To start, a mysterious caller tells you "The president is in danger"... uh ok. Aren't I a steetkid from Night City who has days left to live? Why would I remotely care about the president of this violent, evil, corpo-hellscape of a dystopia I live in? Oh, they are actually a really nice president in this world and not corrupt or cruel and her omni-present ai assistant somehow knew I had a special chip in my head and that only I can help save her... ok... Then 3 minutes later the mystery voice is telling me "Hurry to that ladder V, the yellow one over there, I know you can do this." WTF game am I playing?! The campaigns in a CoD are more original than this and the vibes are completely sanitized and weak. Vocal coaching the player from yellow paint marker to yellow paint marker is the laziest type of game design and completely out of tone of the world of Cyberpunk 2077 too. Just say "Go to there" or "Go to this person" and then let me figure it out like a puzzle using all my cyber enhancements, don't give me 20 progress updates and tell me in a cringe manner how well I'm climbing in a game supposed to be set in a unforgiving gritty world. Anytime you are given freedom you can just sprint and dodge past all the meaningless enemies to trigger the next scripted moment that will reset all of the npc's, unless you are forced into a scripted gunfight you will have to kill everything or a forced stealth part that ultimately devolves into you kill everything. the stakes feel meaningless with checkpoints every 30 seconds and your actions in the world mean nothing and neither do the dialogue options, which gives the game no immersion.

101 hours. Cyberpunk finally defeated me.

I got a lot out of this game, and when Cyberpunk is good, it can be really fun. The combat is great, building out your character and cyberware is addictive, and a lot of the gigs and side missions were easily my favorite parts of the game. They were quick, gave you an objective, let you approach it your way, and then got the hell out of your way.

Unfortunately, once I started focusing on the main story, I hit a wall.

The pacing is absolutely exhausting. Walk with somebody. Listen to them talk. Get in a car. Listen to them talk. Follow somebody. Listen to them talk. Sit down. Listen to them talk. Repeat.

Some of these sequences feel like they go on for 20–30 minutes, and because the game is committed to first person, so much of the storytelling is literally just standing there staring at another character while they dump dialogue on you. There aren't interesting camera angles or cinematic cuts to keep scenes visually engaging. You're just trapped in V's head waiting for people to finish talking.

The braindance sequences were especially miserable for me, and I hated how often the game takes control and momentum away from you for scripted rides, conversations, slow walks, scanning, following characters, and other sequences where you're technically "playing" but barely doing anything.

That's what makes it frustrating, because underneath all of that is a game I actually enjoyed. I loved sneaking into buildings, hacking cameras, throwing knives, using suppressed pistols, upgrading cyberware, experimenting with quickhacks, buying ridiculous cars, and figuring out different ways to clear an objective. When Cyberpunk lets me play Cyberpunk, I like Cyberpunk.

But eventually I realized I was spending too much of my time waiting to get back to the parts I enjoyed.

I even tried Phantom Liberty, unlocked the Relic tree, entered Dogtown, and almost immediately found myself thinking, oh God, more walking and talking.

I wanted to finish the main story. I really did. After 101 hours, I figured I had to. But gaming shouldn't feel like homework, and eventually I realized I was forcing myself to finish something I wasn't enjoying anymore.

So I'm calling it.

Great world. Great combat. Great character-building. Some genuinely fun side content. Terrible pacing, overly long dialogue sequences, too many moments where control is taken away from the player, and storytelling that I found incredibly stale.

After 101 hours, Cyberpunk didn't beat V.

It beat me.

4/10 — Not Recommended.

It's alright. It's definitely entertaining. But it's not the game I was hoping it would be. It's not the "Blade Runner" dark dystopian vibes. It's more "GTA meets Saints Row" vibes. "haha d*ck implants malfunction" vibes. The characters are all caricatures, stereotypes, blown to the extremes. Voice lines sometimes feel like they recorded them out of order over several sessions with no cohesion or flow. You are constantly being slammed by messages and calls and side information but there really isn't that much reason to read it all because there's very little substance to the world building and it feels tedious. It also doesn't feel like you actually change the course of the game at all as often your dialog options are the same but just worded differently. 

If we look at gameplay: the main missions offer a bunch of ways to get the objective done. That's cool. Outside of that there's no dialog options to talk your way out of things. Stealth is not really rewarded and a lot of it is just combat. The combat in itself is pretty alright but at higher difficulty enemies just become spongy and your weapons generally feel quite weak making a human take as many bullets to the head as a full on robot. For a Saints Row game that's what I'd expect. I was hoping for something a little better here.

Overall with the expectation of an immersive dystopian RPG I can't give it more than a 6/10. It's fun. It works well as 'mindless entertainment' (although admittedly there's to much in the sense of unskipable cutscenes / dialog in the game to be purely that.... just the 'intro' to the game took me 4 hours while not doing that much besides getting to the title screen. Dialog where you don't really have options aside from saying the same thing 2 different ways which in the end doesn't matter).

I think the framework for this game is solid. The art direction is very cool. The music is solid. The factions and stuff that's all good. If they every make a part 2 I hope they invest more into it being an actual RPG more akin to Deus Ex or Mass Effect (although... well controversial ending... but that aside) and that they make it a bit more grounded and gritty.

Title: Never Fade Away...

A lot of time has passed since launch, and only now can I truly say it: this game is a masterpiece. The work CD Projekt Red put into turning this around is fantastic.

The plot tackles real, massive issues reflecting our own world. This isn't just a brief main quest that feels like a small add-on to a massive map—it’s a deeply human story filled with heroes, villains, and losers. It asks what it really takes for a "nobody" to become a legend, and more importantly, what price you pay for that success. This is pure, authentic Cyberpunk. To be honest, I wasn't sure CDPR could pull it off, but the voice acting and performances are fabulous. They brought Night City to life so convincingly that you instantly buy into its ruthless rules and struggles.

Gameplay at launch was okay, but weak. Today? It’s phenomenal. The world is packed with hidden details, easter eggs, and its own urban legends. As for bugs, I rarely ran into anything major—just the occasional floating car or clipping geometry. For where the game stands today, it plays great. It just needs a few tiny polish tweaks, but nothing that ruins the experience.

The map is huge, and the DLC filled in every empty space seamlessly. There are countless small stories to uncover and interesting places to explore. The level design and world-building deserve serious praise.

Summary:
Without spoiling anything: trust me, you won't regret playing this. It’s far from a typical video game story—it’s something much deeper. Accept the rules of Night City, jump in, and experience it. The writing and acting ensure this world never feels like a hollow cardboard set; the city is cruel, and you will feel every bit of it.

Counter-Strike 2: A Song of Smoke and Betrayal
Hear ye, hear ye, Lords and Ladies of the Competitive Realm!

Counter-Strike 2 is a battlefield worthy of legends. A game of steel nerves, cunning strategies, and glorious headshots. Here, friendships are forged in fire, rivalries are born in blood, and every round is a tale worthy of the bards. The thrill of clutching a 1v5 is sweeter than victory at the Iron Throne, and the sound of an AWP firing is music to the ears of even the coldest lord of Westeros.

The skins? Oh, what a splendid treasury! From crimson blades worthy of House Lannister to dragon-lore rifles fit for the Targaryens, one may adorn their arsenal in magnificent fashion. For in this realm, it is not merely how you slay your foes, but how gloriously you do so.

The competition is fierce, the stakes are high, and when both teams are evenly matched, the battles are glorious. Every smoke is a scheme, every flash a deception, and every defuse a race against the Stranger himself.

BUT LO, A DARKNESS GATHERS BEYOND THE WALL.

For this realm is plagued by a most vile affliction: the poison of cheaters.

Wallhackers, who see through stone as if blessed by the Three-Eyed Raven. Aimbotters, whose arrows never miss, whose bullets find skulls with the certainty of a prophecy. Suspicious lords who turn corners with knowledge no mortal ought to possess. They roam the servers like White Walkers, corrupting the living and extinguishing the joy of honest warriors.

And what of the honourable player who trains for countless hours, perfects their aim, studies the maps, and fights with all the skill they possess? They are left wondering whether they were bested by a better warrior or struck down by some foul sorcery beyond the laws of the realm.

'Tis a cruel fate, to enter the arena seeking glory, only to discover that the enemy has brought a dragon to a knife fight.

Still, when the stars align, the teams are fair, and the cheaters are banished beyond the Wall, Counter-Strike 2 remains a magnificent contest of skill, teamwork, and nerve.

My verdict, therefore, is this:

A glorious game with the heart of a champion, the soul of a warrior, and the potential to rule the Seven Kingdoms of competitive shooters.

Yet its throne is besmirched by treachery, and its kingdom weakened by those who forsake honour for hollow victories.

Valve, the realm cries out for justice! Sharpen thy anti-cheat, strengthen the Watch, and cast these foul sorcerers into the frozen wastes!

For a kingdom cannot thrive when its honest warriors grow weary of fighting shadows.

Would I recommend it? Aye.

But I would sooner trust a Lannister with my gold than trust every death replay in this cursed realm.

J’ai vraiment bien aimé Cyberpunk 2077. Au début, j’étais pas forcément à fond dans le jeu, mais plus j’avançais, plus j’ai accroché à l’histoire et aux personnages.

Le truc que j’ai le plus aimé, c’est clairement Night City. La ville est énorme et il y a toujours quelque chose à faire. Même quand on ne fait pas l’histoire principale, on peut faire des quêtes secondaires, des contrats, se balader ou juste découvrir la ville. Je trouve que l’ambiance est vraiment réussie, surtout la nuit avec tous les néons et les bâtiments.

L’histoire principale est aussi un gros point fort. J’ai bien aimé suivre V et surtout la relation avec Johnny Silverhand. Il y a pas mal de moments qui restent en tête et certaines missions sont vraiment excellentes. Les personnages secondaires sont aussi assez intéressants et certaines quêtes sont presque aussi bien que les missions principales.

Au niveau du gameplay, j’ai bien aimé avoir plusieurs façons de jouer. On peut utiliser des armes, des armes de corps à corps, le piratage ou jouer plus discrètement. Le système de cyberware permet aussi de rendre son personnage beaucoup plus puissant au fur et à mesure.

Graphiquement, je trouve le jeu encore très beau. Night City est vraiment impressionnante et certains endroits sont magnifiques. Avec de bons réglages graphiques, le jeu peut vraiment être incroyable.

J’ai aussi beaucoup aimé les quêtes secondaires parce qu’elles ne servent pas juste à gagner de l’argent ou de l’expérience. Certaines racontent vraiment des histoires intéressantes et permettent de mieux connaître les personnages.

Pour la durée de vie, je trouve qu’il y a largement de quoi faire. J’ai passé pas mal de temps dessus et je n’ai même pas terminé tout le contenu. Le jeu peut facilement occuper pendant plusieurs dizaines d’heures si on fait aussi les quêtes secondaires.

Pour Phantom Liberty, je ne peux pas encore donner mon avis complet parce que je ne l’ai pas terminé. Pour l’instant, j’aime beaucoup l’ambiance et les nouvelles missions, mais je préfère attendre d’avoir fini le DLC avant de donner une vraie note définitive.

Au final, je donnerais environ **10/10 à Cyberpunk 2077**. C’est un jeu que j’ai vraiment apprécié et dans lequel j’ai passé beaucoup de temps. Il n’est pas parfait, mais son histoire, son univers, ses personnages et tout ce qu’il y a à faire font que j’ai vraiment aimé l’expérience.

Pour Phantom Liberty, pour l’instant je partirais sur **9/10**, mais cette note pourra changer quand je l’aurai terminé.

Rockstar's most refined skinner box. GTA Online has interesting aspects but is ultimately dragged down by greed and spaghetti code. Recent events may come to mind, but the reality is that the writing has been on the wall. Shark cards were always around, servers were peer-to-peer, shareholders had their meetings. It was only a question of "How" Rockstar will try to screw over players, not "If" or even "When". 

As a skinner box, GTA Online acts somewhat like an idle game: Spend time to build up your resources, and use those to get more resources. Higher rank means more weapons and health, higher stats give small but useful benefits, more money lets you buy more content to play as well as more methods to make money. It contrasts from traditional idle games by... being GTA, so to speak.

Of course, the fundamental flaw here is that Rockstar doesn't respect your time. No, it might be better to say that GTA Online is designed to waste as much of your time as possible while you try to make progress. The various businesses players can purchase will take several hours to fill up to capacity, but can easily have all product turned to dust with raids or by encouraging the entire lobby to sabotage sell missions. 

The heists are the best and worst part of Online. The most interesting content by far, self-sabotaged by legacy code, greed, and plain old bad game design. Enemies randomly firing off their entire magazine in one short burst, limited healing that can only be refilled in free roam, challenges that can't be retried from checkpoint, damage reducing payout and said reductions carrying over between checkpoint restarts, and full restarts only being possible by exiting the heist entirely and going back to free roam. 

Not to mention the jury-rigged stealth mechanics that never get fully explained AND have variable rules every time they appear. Some stealth encounters require you to stay pacifist (and don't tell you), and others have guards with a 0 second delay before they alert everyone. Even in the new Kortz Center Heist, the stun gun is silent for the entire heist until you exit the building, where it's so loud that even using a melee takedown will alert guards halfway across the map. 

The two most recent heists, Cayo Perico and the Kortz Center, have severe tonal dissonance. Even ignoring the numbers, they fail to live up to the fantasy of looting of a large island or museum. You can put in the time and effort to do every prep mission, clear every guard and avoid every camera, but in the end each person can only carry a handful of loot. It silently begs the question: Is it really a heist if you leave so much behind?

Rockstar is never going to fix that dissonance, nor do they care to. With the recent patch that came with the Kortz Center Heist, it's clear that Rockstar does not want players to experience GTA Online in any way they please. They want sessions to be weekly, they want players to wait on timers before playing, and they do not want people to experience everything too fast without putting real cash in. 

Considering this is the Legacy version's review, it's worth noting how horribly unstable the netcode is. Infinite loading screens make it nearly impossible to play for half an hour without needing to restart after entering/exiting an interior, moving to a new session, or entering/exiting any mission. Even years ago it wasn't great, but trying to play this recently felt like all the exaggerations you could make about bad netcode coming true.

Even before this patch, I wouldn't recommend getting into GTA Online. It asks for a lot of time and effort from you without giving nearly as much in return. If you really have to play it, find a way to bypass the grind (not with shark cards) and only do whatever catches your eye.

If you're crazy about idle games that hate you but love your wallet, maybe play it. Otherwise, find another game. 

Oh, right. GTA V Story Mode. It's... okay, I guess. The story and characters are nothing to write home about, neither great nor bad enough to say much about. The ending is arbitrarily split into 3 decisions with 2 bad options that no one wants to pick. The gameplay is fine, someone else might find it more appealing but I don't have much to say about it.

GTA V Story Mode is probably worth the price, on sale, but seeing how they've made GTA Online so hostile to its playerbase, Rockstar does not deserve the money.

Cyberpunk 2077 feels like my favorite '90s movies came to life — Blade Runner's neon-noir streets, RoboCop's corporate dystopia, Johnny Mnemonic's data-in-the-skull paranoia, Total Recall's untrustworthy memories. There's Alita's cyborg heart, The Sixth Day's cloning anxiety, Minority Report's surveillance-state advertising, even Stallone's Judge Dredd in the city's brutalist sprawl. The characters feel alive, and the whole thing plays less like a game and more like a prestige TV series — Sons of Anarchy, Breaking Bad. Most games don't touch storytelling on this level. It's superb, and I feel the nostalgia at every turn.

I really really wanted to like this game, but sadly I just can't enjoy it, or even give it the mark of a function/completed game, even after all of the improvements by the devs since release.

I’d highly recommend getting Phantom Liberty as it’s possibly better than the main story. What this game does best is the big missions/heists that feel very cinematic and action-packed. Can’t say many of the characters have a great deal of depth, with the exception of Johnny and Reed who are genuinely well written and multi-faceted.

There’s a fairly solid progression system and ability to approach things different ways - unlike most games, many boss battles including the final boss can be beaten in stealth. I did however find that once I’d found the groove of my playstyle and a few key strong weapons it didn’t change up much after that. In an ideal world there’d be some more unique weapons/perks that allow for some goofy or niche playstyles late game, but I can’t complain too much as there is a fair degree of customisation and progression.

At points I did wish they did lean more into the cyberpunk world gameplay-wise e.g. having a drone companion, or a flying car, or something. At points it did feel like GTA with a futurist late-capitalist skin on it.

However overall, I can highly recommend! Looking forward to Projekt Red’s next game.

Cyberpunk 2077 is still in 2026 a gorgeous game. Night City looks absolutely stunning and on a modern PC you can crank the graphics settings all the way up and still enjoy an incredibly smooth experience. Your GPU may sound like it's preparing for takeoff, but hey, that's a small price to pay for pretty neon lights.

There are plenty of side quests to keep you busy, and some of them are genuinely great. That said, I still found myself wishing there were more. Apparently, I have developed an unhealthy appetite for wandering around Night City doing increasingly ridiculous jobs for complete strangers.

The biggest problem, however, is the main story. It's simply too short. If you focus mostly on the main quests, the game ends before it really feels like you've gotten your money's worth. You spend all this time building your character, exploring Night City and becoming murder machine, only for the main story to basically end too soon.

Thankfully, Cyberpunk 2077 has some solid replay value. You can approach the game with completely different builds, whether you want to be a stealthy hacker, a heavily armed psychopath, a katana-wielding lunatic, or some other combination of questionable life choices. Changing your stats and playstyle can make another playthrough feel surpprisingly different.

Overall, Cyberpunk 2077 is a fantastic-looking and incredibly smooth game with a huge amount of potential content, but I can't help feeling that the main story should have been significantly longer.

8/10 – Would happily return to Night City, preferably after committing several more crimes and spending another 40 hours of doing anything but meeting Hanako at the Embers.

I played GTAV for the first time upon its original release on my PS3, wondering how on Earth that old console was able to process a game like this. And now, as I am writing this review in autumn 2026, GTAVI is coming out next month. Considering that GTAV has sold around 220 million copies by this point, along with all of its re-releases, it has obviously proven itself to be an enormous success in virtually every regard, whether we're talking about critics' reviews or fans' opinions. GTA games have always been a cultural phenomenon and a major force in pushing the boundaries of gameplay, immersion and, especially, vast open worlds. And I think most people would agree that GTAV became the series' highest point in all of these areas. I should note, however, that before GTAIV I personally wasn't a fan of the series for some reason. But GTAIV changed that completely. Its new engine and more realistic approach to almost everything, combined with a serious story and a huge leap in terms of immersion, finally sold me on the series. So, when GTAV was about to be released, I decided to buy a PS3 Super Slim primarily to experience it at launch, as I had previously been a PC gamer. It's crazy to think that this was 13 years ago. So I guess now is the perfect moment to draw some conclusions about GTAV and decide how we will remember this game. Personally, I would say that in many ways this game still holds up remarkably well, despite its dated movement and shooting mechanics, which feel rather clunky by today's standards. But when talking about GTAV, we cannot ignore the elephant in the room: GTA Online. And this is where two completely opposite opinions about GTAV can coexist. There is GTAV's single-player mode: a crime comedy set in a huge and immersive open world that also serves as one of the best portrayals of Los Angeles in a video game, as well as an amazing time capsule of the early 2010s. And then there is GTA Online, a rather controversial multiplayer mode, which was arguably one of the main reasons Rockstar ended up taking 13 years to release GTAVI. Back in 2013, when GTA Online first launched, I genuinely enjoyed it. It felt revolutionary for its time in terms of multiplayer and what could be achieved in an open-world game. But I think many people will agree with me that its monetization eventually ruined a large part of the experience. Not to mention how much Rockstar changed the tone of the game itself through all those updates. A good example would be the heists. The original heists were quite innovative and worked surprisingly well for their time, both in terms of gameplay and immersion. But then Rockstar added the Doomsday Heist, which turned GTA into some kind of absurd spy-drama parody of itself. And, of course, much of the later content was also tied to increasingly aggressive grinding and monetization. To put it simply, today's GTA Online is a bizarre and incredibly grindy experience, filled with flying futuristic cars, flying bikes, Batmobile-like vehicles, and an enormous amount of content locked behind some of the most monotonous grinding imaginable. So, as entertaining and enjoyable as the single-player experience is, the online mode has become almost the complete opposite for me: bloated, bizarre and, ultimately, rather boring. So, this is my final take on GTAV after all these years. And because of me actually playing to get 100% achievement completition, I think it's indeed valid. If you agree with me, feel free to rate this review positively.

For as much fun as I had with this game, there was a lot to criticise and complain about. When you're fighting enemies and sneaking through enemy forts, this game is really good, like a proper successor to Deus Ex. But most of the game is not doing this, you'll spend much more of your time travelling to these locations and watching a lot of cutscenes (braindances are also supremely boring after the first time).

To rub salt into the wound, the story has an interesting premise and good characters but falls flat due to a lack of story/gameplay integration and the story is really short and really one sided. I get that this is called cyberPUNK, but for a role-playing game, you don't get a lot of choice in how you want to play the role of V in this story. If you don't want to be a punk, sorry, V is going to be one whether you like it or not. The story insists on having everything be a grey moral to the point that it lost all of its meaning, but puts its foot down and insists that choosing to side with a Corpo is a bad thing, despite dedicating one third of the story to a Corpo member trying to win you over (his story missions also had the best setpieces). All of the endings fall flat because of this insistence that no ending can be happy, but especially the Corpo ending since, despite all of the endings/routes following a theme of sacrificing something for your survival, that ending has you sacrifice the MOST things to receive the LEAST rewarding, most downer ending of them all. The double standard would be funny if it weren't sad.

I have also found the game to still be somewhat buggy, one I remember a lot is that if you save the story quests for last and level up on the exploration content, you end up with quests not triggering because the game tries to space them out but doesn't have anything to trigger them with. There is also a bad bug with pop-in, maybe due to low RAM allocation. Vehicles don't load in quickly enough, meaning you can't drive until they do, and several times during races I fell through the ground due to the map not loading in quick enough. On another note, it's also really annoying how you NEED a cyberdeck to do any hacking, whereas the Sandevistan is really fun for stealth builds, but having one means not being able to do really basic things like opening doors, especially after they nerfed quick hacks into the dirt.

Overall, get this on a sale. It is a passable looter-shooter/immersive sim hybrid but is bogged down a lot by not having enough cool levels to play through and too much time spent on a weak story with a forced moral message. Otherwise this game costs way too much for what it is.

A Gentle Dystopia

Ah yes, the promised land is finally here. After a botched release and years of updates improving, expanding, and stabilizing the game along with the release of the massive Phantom Liberty expansion. All is forgiven, Polish devs. But is it? As much as there is about Cyberpunk 2077 that I like and as much as I respect the support CD Projekt Red continued to put into it. We need to talk about the massive elephant in the room that never actually left. Borrowed time.

Majora's Mask is probably one of the most famous examples of making time itself part of the gameplay. Even though its three day loop, that doomsday clock is always ticking. The player constantly understands that time has value. For more modern examples, look at games like The Blood of Dawnwalker or Kingdom Come Deliverance II. Neither necessarily hangs one giant doomsday clock over the player in the same way. Instead, time becomes part of the player's agency. Dawnwalker gives you a limited amount of time before the endgame, with quests and major actions advancing that clock. Deliverance II takes a more situational approach, where certain quests and events will move forward without you if you wait too long. Personally, I think Deliverance II takes this idea a little too literally. Persona 5 is another great example. You have a limited calendar and have to decide how to spend it. Do you improve a relationship? Work on yourself? Explore the palace? Prepare for the next major confrontation? All of these systems are asking the player some variation of the same question. What are you going to do with the time you have? And Cyberpunk presents one of the strongest possible versions of that question. When you're dying, what do you do with your time?

Apparently nothing. Get up samurai, we're going drag racing. Get up samurai, we're clearing every gig and side mission on the entire map. Get up samurai, we're going bowling. This is the massive elephant that I don't think gets criticized nearly enough. The story presents V with a very simple and horrifying problem. You are dying. Your life is disintegrating in front of you. The writing becomes emotional. Relationships start forming. People begin attaching themselves to V. Johnny is slowly taking over. Every lead toward a possible cure should feel increasingly desperate. Your entire story is supposedly happening on borrowed time. And then Cyberpunk almost immediately throws that idea out the window. The clock doesn't actually exist. Take as long as you want. Do every gig. Help every fixer. Buy every car. Make every friend. Finish every companion storyline. Explore every corner of Night City. Eventually, whenever you finally feel like it, go choose your ending.

That's not meaningful agency. That's a story telling you that your time is valuable while the game design simultaneously tells you that your time is infinite. And that creates a massive disconnect. Your relationships with people begin to lose weight. Desperately taking gigs because you need money to upgrade your cyberware stops meaning anything because... why not just do everything? Eventually you'll be swimming in money anyway. The writing constantly asks for an emotional response from the people around V. Meanwhile, V suppresses the biggest problem in their life, another identity is literally eating away at their mind, their body, and eventually their entire existence. That should hang over everything. Every relationship. Every choice. Every job. Every conversation with Johnny. Instead, the uncertainty loses its weight. The confrontations with Johnny lose some of their urgency because, at the end of the day, who cares? Johnny, you and me are going bowling, again.

Once again, modders enter the scene. Modders add an actual doomsday clock, progressing V's deterioration according to the in-game passage of time. Other mods add life sim elements like eating, drinking, sleeping and generally maintaining yourself. The most baffling thing about all of this is that the foundations for these systems are already sitting inside the game. There are food vendors everywhere. Vending machines everywhere. You have a bed. You have showers. You can buy multiple apartments and living spaces. These places are presented like somewhere V can return to, decompress, sleep, shower, eat, and temporarily escape Night City. But for what? The game has all these little pieces suggesting that V is supposed to be living in Night City while simultaneously dying inside it, yet almost none of them carry any real mechanical consequence. And that becomes even stranger when you consider how heavily the writing emphasizes borrowed time. Every new person V grows attached to is potentially someone they're going to lose. Every relationship V builds is happening under the shadow of an approaching death. Every lead toward a cure should matter because another day wasted is another day gone. But without any meaningful passage of time, that shadow never really moves. And that's why, even after all the updates, all the fixes, Phantom Liberty, and everything CD Projekt Red poured into this game, part of Cyberpunk 2077 still feels half cooked to this day.

One of the biggest contradictions is still sitting there at the heart of V's story. Untouched. Unfixed. They wrote about a person discovering that their life suddenly has an expiration date, but never implemented the one element that could have made that premise truly meaningful. Your life is supposed to be on borrowed time. The grim story of a dystopian hell where one person is desperately trying to find some meaning in the trash heap around them loses much of its weight when the game refuses to make time matter. For all the work CD Projekt Red has done rebuilding Cyberpunk 2077, this contradiction has been sitting there since the beginning.

Cyberpunk 2077 is a story rich RPG featuring a beautiful open world, with the best character writing I've seen. The game covers themes such as freedom, identity, greed, and social inequality. It's an unforgettable experience worth playing. Jackie Welles & Johnny Silverhand are [b] GOATED [/b] support characters!

Story: You play as V, a lone merc in Night City, a futuristic violent dystopia dictated by greedy capitalist mega-corporations. You take on the most dangerous jobs trying to stay alive and make a name for yourself. There are 3 life paths to choose from: Nomad, Streetkid, and Corpo. They don't make much of a difference gameplay-wise, aside from unique dialogue options and shaping V's perspective on the world. After your biggest high stakes job goes FUBAR, the story truly begins as you race against time for your life! 

Gameplay: This game feels like a mixture of GTA and Borderlands because of the interactivity, stores, looting, class building, and the leeway to play however you like. Unfortunately, some elements are not well polished, but its not that bad because they can be fixed with mods. Majority of the cars handle terribly! I got around the map 90% of the time using motorcycles because they're really fast and consistently handle well. Another thing I did not enjoy too much was the early game. Enemies scale heavily to your level at all times, so the beginning is kind of rough because your guns aren't strong and targets feel tanky. Shotguns, revolvers, and snipers became my go to weapons. You'll be fine if your aim and positioning is really good. Mid to late game is when you can really start going crazy. 

Environment: Along with the story, this is another great aspect because of its visual storytelling. It shows you how bad things are, instead of telling you. The city is plagued with advertisements, some even reaching the sky! Gangs rule certain city districts, crime thrives more often in some places, and you can really see the poverty and flourishment of areas. What I truly did love were the small mentions of the 2076 Edgerunners crew. You can find iconic items left behind by a few members which is very cool, it makes the city's history feel more connected on a deeper level.

Side Quests: There are many to do and they give you really good rewards, but they aren't special because they follow a repetitive format. The only good quests are the character story missions, these deepen your bond with key characters, allowing you to learn their history and help them out with personal troubles. 

TL;DR Cyberpunk 2077 is one of the best story rich RPG games you can ever play. It has some issues gameplay wise, but they're relatively minor and won't hurt your overall experience. Never stop fighting, my chooms!

Game just does not feel finished. There are still tons of bugs and I will list a couple of the most common/memorable at the end of my review. 

My three general complaints are: 
1. You level up way to fast to the point where it feels punishing to play the hacker playstyle. Every mission you can kill everybody no matter what by only clicking a few buttons. I do think this is a general game issue because the game feels very easy even on the highest difficulty. The only real challenge is when I tell myself "I will only use [x] weapon for this mission." Some enemies have "resistances" to certain forms of combat, but attaching that to the ram system negates it due to the many ways to regen ram or overcharge mode, which allows you to sacrifice hp to hack increasing your ram pool near infinitely. 
2. I don't know if this is just me, but the main story fails to entertain me. This is okay because the side missions are honestly more fun than the busywork the main missions provide. Too much dialogue, too much following frustratingly slow NPCs, and too many tasks and decisions that feel unimportant. 
3. Lastly I know its hard to make games look good while flying; but having flying cars around, millions of dollars in the bank, and being unable to buy one feels kinda bad for a futuristic game. 

All that being said: The world has amazing atmosphere. Driving around, especially in the rain or at night, feels just amazing. The music, the views, and just something I cant explain gives me a amazing feeling of being small... of peace. I do wish there were driving sounds though. 

Here is a list of bugs I have experienced so far. 
1. Picking up items or opening a chest frequently causes things to go flying.
2. NPCs t-posing while driving their cars.
3. Story NPCs get hit by cars during cutscenes causing their dead bodies to drag on the floor while talking to me until they start a different animation and get revived.
4. Enemies glitching into walls and floors.
5. Enemies seeing you through walls and floors.
6. Once a enemy I killed glitched so hard his body was shot into the sky while his head was stuck on a railing causing his entire model to be a massive tapestry spanning over a block and crashing my FPS till it unloaded.
7. Cyberpsycho missions, while being some of the most fun, are also insanely buggy with their triggers. Three times I have had to fast travel, skip 48 hours in time, and then go back just to have things spawn or trigger.
8. Constant floating items, occasional floating NPCs, and briefly floating cars before they crash down. 

The bugs are the main reason I just cannot recommend this game. They break immersion more than anything else.

They forgot to put the game in Cyberpunk.

I've been playing through the story for about six hours now, and I think I've seen half an hour of actual gameplay.
The rest of the time has been spent on the intro, endless dialogues, tutorials, driving sequences (which can run on autopilot — no interaction required), and a “Braindance” — which basically means dragging sliders until the game tells you you've done it right.

At times, it feels like you’re playing a one-button game where you’re constantly pressing the “Next” button. This is often the highlighted dialogue option, opening a menu, walking into a trigger, or buying an item. Considering that you’re basically just pressing “Next” the whole time, the key bindings are absolutely bonkers. For example, there are three different buttons for drawing/holstering your weapon on foot and in a vehicle. Why this isn’t just a simple toggle key is beyond me.

You’re constantly forced to wait: Wait for dialogue, wait for the scanner, wait for a cutscene, wait for an elevator, wait until the NPC has walked somewhere. Think I’m exaggerating? Pay attention to how often the current task says something like “wait for … to happen” or how often you’re presented with a progress bar. The only progress bar I expect to see in games Is the loading screen and that should be as quick as possible.

Combat feels both overloaded and one-dimensional at the same time: You’re shown all kinds of stealth and melee mechanics, but you don’t need them at all — you just end up shooting everyone in the face. If you’re playing stealth, the loop goes: Kill, quicksave, kill, quicksave, quickload if you’re spotted, repeat. And then there’s this thing where the game teases you in the intro that you could perform a simultaneous takedown with your companion. Turns out it’s not part of the missions — it only happens when it’s scripted.

The gunplay is somewhat reminiscent of loot shooters like Borderlands, where enemies are bullet sponges and headshots aren’t lethal. Instead, you end up grinding just to get that one upgrade that lets you reload 20% faster—something you should have from the start, so the gameplay isn’t so terribly sluggish. If you can’t take out an enemy from a distance, you just run right up to them and blast them in the face with the shotgun. In any serious shooter, you’d be dead in seconds. But not in Cyberpunk. And this is on Hard. It’s topped off with a bit of hacking, which means you can make enemies explode or stun them just by clicking on them.

Unfortunately, the story hasn't really grabbed me so far either. There are a lot of people who want to hurt you. You die twice. There's a heist, and they implant some stuff in your brain. That's mainly because of the uninteresting characters. We've got Hispano B.J. Blazkovicz and a handful of other plastic buddies, all of whom are way to talkative and never get to the point. If the dialogue options have serious consequences, the game doesn’t convey that very well.
I experienced a bunch of soft locks already where a npc just would not enter his trigger and the mission would not continue.
[Edit ~20h] In the mission "Never Fade Away" I experienced frequent crashes.

It’s all a real shame, because I thought The Witcher 3 was absolutely fantastic.
The lighting is nice, though. Just like the sound design. It can get a little busy at times. But overall, the technical aspects are pretty good.

I’ll keep on playing. If people say the story is good, there must be something to it. Maybe I’ll find the fun at some point. Maybe John Wick will cheer me up. But then again why does it take a game like this 6 hours to present something interesting? I could have played an entire other game with actual interaction at that time.

[Edit at 10 hours]
I found a scene that’s symptomatic of cyberpunk:
In a brothel, you have a conversation with a prostitute. The goal is to get some information. During this conversation, you’re bombarded with calendar quotes:
“You’re scared because you have given up on your dreams.”
“Not a single thing in this world isn’t in the process of becoming something else.”
“Fear is our weapon in the fight against death.”
"But everything has its end."
The conversation is so generic: if you replace V with $Name and Night City with $Location, you could insert it into any series or game. I suspect you’re supposed to learn something about V’s character, but you don’t. What makes this even more absurd is that you can bypass the scene from the very beginning by saying the safeword (even though you are not in an extreme situation). 
What some might call “building atmosphere,” I consider a waste of time. There are so many games that manage to portray deep characters and atmosphere without trapping you in hours of fluff dialogue.
This scene lasts 5 or 6 minutes. After that, you have to move on to the next cutscene.

[Edit at 32 hours]
The final mission does not have any gameplay either. [spoiler] You can just decide to kill yourself. V probably should have done that right at the start, That would have been a lot less painful. [/spoiler]

Cyberpunk 2077 is, in my opinion, the best story-driven RPG I've played in years. What makes it so special is that every part of the game feels carefully crafted. The main story is emotional, gripping, and filled with unforgettable moments, but what truly surprised me was the quality of the side content. Unlike many open-world games where side quests feel like repetitive filler, Cyberpunk's side missions are so well-written and unique that they often feel like they could be part of the main storyline. Many of them introduce memorable characters, unexpected twists, and meaningful choices that make every mission worth playing.

The attention to detail is simply incredible. Night City is one of the most immersive worlds I've ever explored. Every district has its own identity, architecture, atmosphere, and people. The city constantly feels alive, with crowds walking the streets, traffic moving through highways, advertisements covering every building, and countless small details that make the world believable. Even the Badlands outside the city have their own unique atmosphere, making the contrast between the urban chaos and the empty desert feel natural and immersive.

Visually, Cyberpunk 2077 is absolutely stunning. The lighting, weather effects, reflections, animations, and overall art direction make almost every location look like it belongs in a sci-fi movie. Whether you're driving through the neon-lit streets at night or watching the sunrise over the Badlands, the game is full of breathtaking moments.

The RPG systems are another reason why I love this game. The skill tree gives you the freedom to create completely different builds depending on how you want to play. You can become a deadly Netrunner who hacks enemies from a distance, a stealth assassin using throwing knives and silenced weapons, a cyber-enhanced samurai with katanas, or a heavily armored tank charging into combat with shotguns and LMGs. Cyberware implants, perks, iconic weapons, and countless equipment combinations make character progression incredibly satisfying.

Replayability is another area where Cyberpunk truly shines. Every new playthrough can feel completely different thanks to the different lifepaths, dialogue options, character builds, romances, endings, and even your character's gender. The choices you make throughout the game often change conversations, relationships, and the way certain missions unfold, giving you plenty of reasons to experience the story multiple times.

What really sets Cyberpunk 2077 apart is how all of these systems come together. The outstanding writing, unforgettable characters, meaningful side quests, incredible attention to detail, gorgeous visuals, deep progression systems, and the living, breathing world create an experience that feels unique from beginning to end. Very few games manage to combine storytelling, gameplay, exploration, and role-playing this well, which is exactly why I consider Cyberpunk 2077 the best RPG I've played in a very long time.
